title: Name each thing for what it is
statement: In narration, name a representation as a representation, give the category before a proper name, and say when something shown is not an example of what is being taught.
detail: The read-aloud checklist of an intro-video BrainLift for a Grade 3 reading course asks of every beat whether a representation is named as one, since a child otherwise takes a statue for the person it shows; whether the category arrives before the proper noun ("Two of those cities, called Ur and Uruk"), so the name lands as an instance of something already understood; and whether a non-example is named as one, since a lizard shown during a beat about mammals reads as a mammal unless somebody says it is not (`downloads/BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md`, lines 349 to 351). It is a house checklist, run aloud by a person against the storyboard; no outcome was measured.

evidence.path: BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md
evidence.quote: Example: "That is a statue of a pharaoh", never "that is a pharaoh". A child otherwise takes the object for the person.

evidence.path: BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md
evidence.quote: The name then lands as an instance of something already understood rather than as a new thing to hold.

evidence.path: BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md
evidence.quote: If something on screen is not an example of what is being taught, say so.
Imagery on a teaching screen must not create a false instance of the concept being taught.
